{'translation': 'The Hong Kong Observatory noted that over the broad low-pressure trough in the northern part of the South China Sea, a low-pressure area is gradually developing and moving closer to the Guangdong coast. As the associated convective cloud clusters are currently concentrated to the south, more time is needed for consolidation, and whether it will develop into a tropical depression can only be determined when it approaches the Guangdong coast. The Observatory said that if the low-pressure area develops into a tropical depression, it will assess whether to issue the Standby Signal No. 1 from this evening (July 13) to early tomorrow morning (July 14).'}

{'translation': 'The Observatory also stated that, according to current forecasts, the low-pressure system will be closest to Hong Kong tomorrow morning, passing within a range of 100 kilometres. Heavy showers, thunderstorms and squalls are expected tomorrow (the 14th), and it may be necessary to issue the Rainstorm Warning Signal or the Localised Heavy Rain Advisory. Strong winds will prevail offshore, and some low-lying areas may experience flooding. On Wednesday (July 15), rain will be heavy at times initially and winds will remain strong offshore.'}

{'translation': "The Observatory expects Hong Kong's typhoon season this year to run from June to October. This year's first Standby Signal No. 1 was issued on July 2 due to the approach of Severe Tropical Storm Maysak over the South China Sea, which brought over 30 millimetres of rainfall to many parts of Hong Kong the following day; Maysak had once passed some 600 kilometres to the southwest of Hong Kong."}
